entries.name: Emperor penguin
behaviour: males incubate one egg on their feet through the polar night
pack into huddles that rotate the outermost birds
colonies on fast ice, forming and breaking up with the season
entries.notes: The only bird that breeds through the Antarctic winter on the sea ice. The huddle is the model, not the individual: a colony reads as a rippling black mass with individual shapes inside it.

entries.name: Adélie penguin
behaviour: pebble nest scrape defended by both parents
leaping onto ice shelves from below, a built-in jump animation
mass commuting along ice channels to open water

voxel_model.pattern: black hood, white eye-ring and chest

entries.notes: The bold white-eye-ringed everyman of Antarctic colonies; bold enough to steal pebbles from the nest next door. Easy to animate with a fast, rocking waddle and a head-bobbing walk.

entries.name: Gentoo penguin
behaviour: fastest swimming penguin, porpoise-leaping at speed
recognises mates and chicks by voice among thousands
walks with a tail-high waddle and loud trumpeting
entries.notes: White bonnet, orange bill, tail held high: the most personable of the penguins in one voxel. Swimming at 20 km/h is the best water speed of any penguin in the game.

entries.name: Chinstrap penguin
behaviour: lays pebble nests on ice-free rock with sooty, smoky backs
colonies can carpet whole islands
snow-bare volcanic slopes are favourite breeding ground

voxel_model.pattern: black helmet band under the bill

entries.notes: Named for the thin black chin-strap across white cheeks. Huge colonies make it the most common large bird in parts of the peninsula.

entries.name: Weddell seal
behaviour: keeps breathing holes open in the ice with saw-like teeth
dives 600 m deep and stays under for over an hour
sings under the ice; the song carries through fast ice like a drum
entries.notes: The most southerly breeding mammal on Earth, and the icon of the fast ice itself. In Erebus Bay, McMurdo Sound, it is effectively the only mammal.

entries.name: Crabeater seal
entries.migrates: follows the seasonal pack ice edge
behaviour: sieve-like multicusped teeth strain krill from seawater
most numerous seal on Earth, an estimated 7-15 million animals
pale coat with a sharp dark stripe, built for pack-ice camouflage
entries.notes: A seal that lives almost entirely on krill; the sieve-teeth are the one detail worth modelling closely. Likely the most populous seal species on the planet.

entries.name: Leopard seal
entries.migrates: seasonal, follows the pack ice edge
behaviour: females up to 1.5 times the mass of males
solitary ambush predator waiting at ice-edge swim channels
whips penguins back and forth to strip skin and flippers

voxel_model.pattern: spotted dark mantle like a leopard

entries.notes: The apex hunter of the ice edge; the one animal a swimming player should genuinely dread. Efficient krill feeder as well as an ambush penguin killer.

entries.name: Southern elephant seal
behaviour: bulls inflate a proboscis and roar to claim harems
dive to 1,000 m and stay under for nearly two hours
time ashore in massive colonies twice a year, the rest at sea
entries.notes: Largest pinniped alive; a bull is a wall of blubber with a breathing snout. Slaughter history makes drop rates delicate game-design territory.

entries.name: Antarctic fur seal
behaviour: thick pelt of waterproof guard hairs over dense undercoat
males defend harems on ice-free beaches
females fast ashore for days, then make long foraging trips at sea
entries.notes: Nearly hunted to extinction for the pelt, back in the millions now. A recovering colony carpets the beaches and the males bark at anything.

entries.name: Killer whale
behaviour: Antarctic type B packs of 4 to 10 whales wave-wash seals off ice floes
highly cultural: pods have unique dialects and hunting traditions
matriarch-led pods, sons never leave their mother

voxel_model.pattern: white eye patches and oval saddle on black

entries.notes: The wave-washing seal hunt is the single best cinematic moment this biome offers. Two Antarctic ecotypes differ in size and prey: model type A and B only if resources allow.

entries.name: Polar bear
entries.migrates: nomadic, follows the freezing and thawing sea ice
behaviour: smells seals through half a metre of snow
waits stock-still at breathing holes for ringed seals
pregnant females dig dens and sleep through the darkest winter
entries.notes: The undisputed icon of the north ice sheet; the only great bear that hunts on sea ice. A player meeting one at a seal hole gets a survival encounter, not a fight.

entries.name: Arctic fox
behaviour: follows polar bears to scavenge carcass remains
blue-morph and white-morph both occur; coat flips with the season
caches food in permafrost for winter
entries.notes: The cleaner of the polar bear's kills and the mascot of the north. A white, plump, trotting shape at the ice edge sells the biome instantly.

entries.name: Snowy owl
behaviour: hunts by day from a low perch or by hovering
can raise large broods only in lemming peak years
big yellow eyes; the whitest of all owls
entries.notes: The daylight owl of the high north; its irruption years push thousands south into the steppe. Watch it from a distance, perched on a boulder above the snow.

entries.name: Gyrfalcon
behaviour: largest falcon; chases prey in level flight rather than stooping
white, grey and dark morphs all occur, the white being the famous arctic one
pairs hunt cliff-nesting birds along the coast
entries.notes: The king of the north falcons. A circling white gyrfalcon above a guillemot cliff is the most regal small thing the biome can show.

entries.name: Walrus
entries.migrates: follows the sea ice freeze and thaw
behaviour: hauls out in vast crowded colonies on ice floes and beaches
uses tusks to anchor on ice and rake up clams from the seabed
roars and clacks with pipe-organ bells echoing through fog

voxel_model.pattern: wrinkled brown hide, long ivory tusks

entries.notes: Both seafloor dredge and ice-anchor, tusks and all. Crowded, noisy, whiskered haul-outs are the counterpart to the elephant seal beaches of the south.

entries.name: Ringed seal
behaviour: keeps breathing holes open with strong claws, sometimes through a metre of ice
pups are born in snow lairs on the ice, safe from wind and bears
the polar bear's staple prey across the whole Arctic
entries.notes: The base of the polar bear's diet and the reason bears travel the ice at all. Pup lairs under drift snow are a huntable detail for a stealthy player.

entries.name: Bearded seal
behaviour: the Arctic's famous singing seal: long, eerie underwater trills
bottom-feeds on shelled benthic animals with heavily bristled whiskers
solitary, wary, usually the isolated seal on an ice floe
entries.notes: The singer: if the ice has a soundtrack, it is the bearded seal's trill. Model it as the solitary floe seal in the polar bear's proximity.

entries.name: Harp seal
entries.migrates: long migrations between whelping ice patches and feeding grounds
behaviour: pups are born with pure white coats on the spring ice
whitecoats were once harvested on the ice in huge numbers
gathers in vast migratory herds moving along the ice edge

voxel_model.pattern: black harp saddle on silver back

entries.notes: White newborn pups against dark ice made this species infamous. In spring the whelping patches turn into a bustle of white fluff on dark ice.

entries.name: Narwhal
entries.migrates: seasonal, through ice leads into summer fjords
behaviour: males carry a single spiralling ivory tusk, up to 3 m long
summer in dense aggregations under ice leads
can dive to 1,500 m under the fast ice
entries.notes: The unicorn of the Arctic. The tusk is the point of the model; everything else is a torpedo with flukes and speckles.

entries.name: Beluga whale
entries.migrates: seasonal, between summer estuaries and ice-covered winter seas
behaviour: pure white adults with a bulbous melon; born grey
'canary of the sea', constantly calling to its pod
can turn its head and has no dorsal fin, slipping under ice
entries.notes: The white whale: vocal, friendly-looking, and an expert ice-lead navigator. Summer estuary flocks can number in the thousands.

entries.name: Black-legged kittiwake
behaviour: nests on narrow cliff ledges over the sea
the classic 'kit-tee-waaake' call gives every cliff a voice
huge declines where forage fish disappear
entries.notes: The voice of the Arctic cliff: white cliffs where a million pairs hang their nests above the surf. Colonies are loud enough to hear from a boat kilometres away.

entries.name: Brünnich's guillemot
behaviour: nests on bare ledges, egg pear-shaped so it rolls in a circle, not off
dives 100 m deep for fish, wing-flapping through water
in winter, dense rafts gather far out at sea
entries.notes: The thick-billed murre: a black-and-white vertical torpedo on cliff ledges. Chicks jump from ledges into the sea when still unable to fly.

entries.name: Little auk
behaviour: the smallest auk, the size of a starling, packed in millions on cliff slopes
alkefjeldet-type colonies are bird-white from the scree
harlequin-plumage winter, black and white
entries.notes: A starling on an Arctic cliff; an Alkefjeldet colony is millions of these chirping on black scree. The densest bird aggregation the north has.

entries.name: Glaucous gull
behaviour: the big pale thug of the Arctic: pale wingtips, no black at all
raided nests, took guillemot chicks from parents
follows bears and humans for carrion
entries.notes: The big, pale Arctic cleanup crew. If a polar bear kills a ringed seal, a glaucous gull will be standing on it by the time the bear leaves.

entries.name: South polar skua
entries.migrates: migrates north to the tropics in the austral winter
behaviour: patrols breeding colonies and kills penguin chicks when parents leave
bold against people: dives at the heads of walking researchers
pairs defend territories on bare ground among the penguin colonies

voxel_model.pattern: dark overall, pale flashes at the wing base

entries.notes: The dive-bombing pirate of Antarctic colonies. Walk near a nest with its back turned and it will clip your head; its scream is the sound every Antarctic field researcher knows.

entries.name: Antarctic tern
entries.migrates: pole-to-pole, the longest migration of any bird
behaviour: migrates from the Antarctic to the Arctic and back each year, chasing summer
dives on fish from a cruising hover
nests in dense colonies on the ice-free ground

voxel_model.pattern: black cap, long tail streamers, red bill

entries.notes: The longest commuter on Earth: Antarctic nest to Arctic feed and back to catch both summers. Its screaming dive-bombed colonies are a classic research-station hazard.

entries.name: Snow petrel
entries.migrates: winter refuge; feeds along the ice edge
behaviour: the whitest bird of Antarctica, glowing against dark rock
breeds only on the ice-free cliff stains of the inner continent
dives and surface-seizes along leads in pack ice
entries.notes: A ghost-white gull-shaped wand on the inner continent; only seen streaking low across the pack ice or on the rare ice-free cliff.

entries.name: Antarctic petrel
entries.migrates: winter dispersal north of the pack ice
behaviour: gathers in vast aggregations along the pack ice edge
flies low and skims krill from the surface
colonies crowd together on barren rock in the inner continent
entries.notes: A smoky gull with a pale belly; vast packs gather at the edge of the ice where the krill are. A feeding flock can tint a bay grey.

entries.name: Wilson's storm petrel
entries.migrates: migrates to the northern hemisphere each austral winter
behaviour: jaunts over the waves with dangling legs, like a dancing spider
arguably the most abundant seabird on Earth
storm petrels breed in rock crevices on ice-free coasts and islands

voxel_model.pattern: black body, white rump flash, yellow-webbed feet

entries.notes: A swallow-sized bird that looks like a hummingbird on a string. Around ships it is the first bird on the scene, walking on water.

entries.name: Ross seal
behaviour: the rarest and least known of the Antarctic seals
tilts its head back to display a striped throat when threatened
its eerie song, heard under pack ice, is the 'singing seal' of icebreaker lore

voxel_model.pattern: silver neck stripes, reddish face markings

entries.notes: The least known seal: rarely seen, rarely photographed, famous only for its song and its throat display. A properly surprising find deep in the pack ice.

entries.name: Ivory gull
entries.migrates: wanders with the ice; flocks south in lean winters
behaviour: follows polar bears and kayak hunters to scavenge kills
nests in tiny colonies on high cliff ledges, unreachable to land predators
threatened by contaminants and loss of ice habitat

voxel_model.pattern: pure white with a near-black bill

entries.notes: The 'sea ghost': a pure-white gull trailing polar bears. Where the ice is a working landscape of kills and leftovers, this bird is the specialist for it.

entries.name: Antarctic krill
entries.migrates: diel vertical migration, up at night to feed, down by day
behaviour: feeds on algae scraped from the underside of sea ice
swarms can cover hundreds of square kilometres
swarms fluoresce; penguins dive into the glow
entries.notes: The foundation of the entire Antarctic food web: baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish all hang on this one shrimp. Model it as a dense shimmering cloud, not as individuals.

entries.name: Antarctic silverfish
behaviour: the dominant fish of Antarctic shelf waters; over 90% of the fish biomass at McMurdo Sound
schools hover below sea ice, moving with the light
feeds on copepods, feeding nearly everything else in turn
entries.notes: The one small fish the whole continent runs on; a penguin's winter dinner. In game terms, the food chain's load-bearing block is a 12 cm silver torpedo.

entries.name: Antarctic toothfish
behaviour: lives at crushing depths, 2,000 m and below, under the Ross Ice Shelf
the fish behind the 'Chilean sea bass' fishery
slow-growing, slow to replace; fought over by industry and science
entries.notes: The monster of the deep shelf; a metre and a half of muscular fish. Also the one fish hunted hard commercially in the Southern Ocean.

entries.name: Greenland shark
behaviour: the longest-lived vertebrate known, living three to five centuries
nearly blind: a parasite in the eye is so common it is nearly universal
drifts up to the surface at night in the shallows
entries.notes: A shark older than some tree lines. One that swam past an Inuit hunter in 1700 is plausibly still cruising the fjords; game's best candidates for a truly ancient deep-drop encounter.

entries.name: Colossal squid
behaviour: the heaviest invertebrate on Earth; the confirmed record is 495 kg
hunts in the dark 2,000 m depths with enormous swivelled eyes
its long hooked clubs and beaks are the source of the sperm whale's scarred face
entries.notes: The deep-sea monster of the south; only scarred from sperm whale beaks, rarely seen. An endgame encounter for anyone mad enough to dive under the Ross Ice Shelf.
